title: Burning Scrolls to Read the Unreadable: A 2,000-Year-Old Mystery
summary:
Douglas Seiler went to unusual lengths to recreate an ancient mystery. He obtained papyrus and reed pens from Egypt, along with traditional lampblack ink from Japan. Then he paid high school students to write on the papyrus using passages from "Star Wars," the Bible, and a quote from the 1960s sci-fi show "The Outer Limits." Finally, he burned them.

The experiment mimicked a catastrophe that occurred nearly 2,000 years ago in Herculaneum, an ancient Roman city. When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E., volcanic ash overwhelmed the city and transformed more than a thousand papyrus scrolls in a local library into fragile, charred remains. The same eruption buried nearby Pompeii. Yet the destruction also produced an extraordinary form of preservation. The Herculaneum collection is the only known intact library to survive from antiquity, potentially preserving works that have otherwise vanished.

Seiler wanted to know whether researchers could recover writing from these carbonized scrolls without physically unrolling them — an action that could cause the brittle papyrus to crumble into black dust. His idea focused on the chemistry of the ink. If some ancient inks contained lead, he reasoned, that metal might absorb X-rays far more strongly than the surrounding carbonized papyrus. A computer could then use the scans to virtually flatten the sheets and expose the hidden writing.

In a paper published Sept. 16 in PLOS ONE, Seiler and his collaborators report that the strategy works. Even extremely small amounts of lead made characters detectable with X-ray tomography, also called X-ray CT. Lead absorbed as much as 25 times more X-rays than the burned papyrus around it. "With lead in the ink, you would get a huge friggin' signature," Seiler said. "They're having problems reading a lot of them because of the low contrast of carbon ink on carbon paper. We're relatively certain that if they start searching for lead, or they let us search for lead, it will help this whole process. This is the Holy Grail."

The researchers also found that a relatively inexpensive handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner could detect lead-based ink in a burned scroll. That could screen ancient scrolls and identify the most promising candidates for detailed X-ray CT imaging. Only a small number of the charred scrolls have been virtually opened so far. None were first tested for lead. But at least one previous researcher detected lead in a fragment from early attempts to physically open the scrolls — attempts that often reduced them to ash.

Every scroll successfully opened physically contained writing previously unknown to scholars, many by Philodemus, an Epicurean philosopher. Today, about 1,800 scrolls and fragments survive in Italy, France, and England. "Almost everything from antiquity has been destroyed," Seiler said. "But some of the Herculaneum scrolls aren't copies. These are books directly from the ancient world frozen in time." For scholars, the potential importance is hard to overstate. "The value in this project is practically unquantifiable," said Leah Packard-Grams, a papyrologist at Berkeley. "The stakes are the largest in the history of Greek literature."
why_it_matters: If scanning can recover writing from scrolls too fragile to open, it could restore plays, histories and philosophy lost for two millennia — and the same non-destructive techniques are already being applied to other damaged documents and artifacts, changing what historians can ever hope to read.

background_read: In 79 C.E., Mount Vesuvius (a volcano in southern Italy) erupted and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and volcanic rock. Herculaneum's Villa of the Papyri — a luxury seaside house that scholars have linked to the family of Julius Caesar's father-in-law — held the only intact library known to survive from the ancient world: more than a thousand papyrus scrolls, carbonized into black, brittle lumps. Papyrus itself is a paper-like material made from reed stems that grow along the Nile.

Because the scrolls crumble at a touch, early attempts to open them by hand often destroyed them. That is why researchers now use tools borrowed from medicine and materials science: X-ray tomography (the same CT scanning hospitals use, which builds 3D images from many X-ray pictures) and X-ray fluorescence (which reveals which chemical elements a material contains).

In recent years a competition called the Vesuvius Challenge has awarded prizes to teams using scans and machine learning to read the scrolls without opening them, and several lines of Greek text have already been recovered from the charred lumps. Among the works found so far are writings by Philodemus, a first-century-BCE follower of Epicurus, the Greek philosopher who taught that the greatest pleasure is calm and freedom from pain.

perspectives.description: For classicists this is close to a miracle: the Herculaneum library is the only intact ancient library known, and every scroll opened so far has contained text previously unknown. A cheap lead-screening step could tell researchers which of the roughly 1,800 surviving scrolls are worth the expensive scans, massively speeding up discovery.

The headline result comes from burned modern papyrus written with deliberately chosen inks, not from the ancient scrolls themselves — and none of the carbonized scrolls virtually opened so far were first tested for lead. There is also the risk of hype: if most ancient inks used little or no lead, the method may help only a minority of texts.

This fits a broader pattern of technology reviving lost texts: multispectral imaging revealed the Archimedes Palimpsest, and medical-style CT scanning has been used to read sealed documents and mummy wrappings. Each new imaging tool expands what counts as a readable source.

The practical next step is a systematic lead survey of the surviving scrolls and fragments in Italy, France and England, followed by targeted X-ray CT on the best candidates. Competitions such as the Vesuvius Challenge show how prizes and open data can pull machine-learning researchers into humanities problems.
